claim: T cells in vivo migrate primarily via undirected random walks.
source: T cells in vivo migrate primarily via undirected random walks, but it remains unresolved how these random walks generate an efficient search.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about T cell behavior.

claim: There is substantial cell-to-cell variability in speed among T cells, which persists over timespans of a few hours.
source: there is substantial cell-to-cell variability in speed, which persists over timespans of a few hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and detailed in the results section.

claim: T cells do not perform Levy flight.
source: We show that cells do not perform Levy flight
evidence: This is supported by multiple analyses including MSD, velocity power spectrum, and bout length distributions presented in Figure 1.

claim: There is a correlation between speed and directional persistence in T cells.
source: This variability is amplified by a correlation between speed and directional persistence
evidence: This is demonstrated through data analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The behavioral manifold is preserved under a perturbation to cell speeds.
source: generating a characteristic cell behavioral manifold that is preserved under a perturbation to cell speeds
evidence: This is demonstrated through drug perturbation experiments with Rockout (Figure 5).

claim: The behavioral manifold is seen in Mouse T cells.
source: generating a characteristic cell behavioral manifold that is preserved under a perturbation to cell speeds, and seen in Mouse T cells and Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of published data from Gérard et al., 2014 (Figure 5C-D).

claim: The behavioral manifold is seen in Dictyostelium.
source: generating a characteristic cell behavioral manifold that is preserved under a perturbation to cell speeds, and seen in Mouse T cells and Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of published data from Dang et al., 2013 (Figure 5E-F).

claim: The combination of speed variability and speed-persistence coupling generates a broad range of length scales over which cells explore in vivo.
source: Together, these effects generate a broad range of length scales over which cells explore in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of effective diffusion constants across speed classes (Figure 4B).

claim: For naive T cells within T cell zones, unguided random walk processes dominate migration.
source: However, for naive T cells within T cell zones, in situ imaging studies have found that unguided random walk processes dominate (Miller et al., 2002; Miller et al., 2003; Preston et al., 2006; Cahalan and Parker, 2008; Beltman et al., 2007; Banigan et al., 2015; Harris et al., 2012; Worbs et al., 2007; Textor et al., 2011; Beauchemin et al., 2007; Mrass et al., 2006; Katakai et al., 2013; Mrass et al., 2017, reviewed in Mrass et al., 2010; Krummel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior imaging studies.

claim: T cells must dwell at scales of microns to make contact with antigen presenting cells.
source: T cells must dwell at scales of microns to make contact with antigen presenting cells (Wülfing et al., 1997; Krummel et al., 2000; Beltman et al., 2009a; Fricke et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: T cells must migrate over scales of millimeters to find rare targets.
source: yet migrate over scales of millimeters to find rare targets.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for T cell function based on biological context.

claim: A conventional diffusive random walk struggles to access varied scales efficiently.
source: A conventional diffusive random walk struggles to access these varied scales efficiently, since a walker that dwells near another cell for 1 min would require several days to travel 1 mm.
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations about diffusive processes.

claim: T cells may have an intrinsic behavioral program that allows them to explore over different length scales.
source: Several authors have suggested that T cells may have an intrinsic behavioral program that allows them to explore over different length scales (Harris et al., 2012; Krummel et al., 2016; Mempel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature.

claim: Observation over short periods cannot distinguish between Levy flight and heterogeneity amongst individual walkers.
source: However, observation over short periods cannot distinguish between Levy flight and heterogeneity amongst individual walkers (Petrovskii et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: The observed T cells are in tissue in the tail of the zebrafish, primarily in the tail fin and larval fin fold.
source: We observed a population of motile cells in tissue in the tail of the zebrafish, primarily in the tail fin and larval fin fold (Figure 1A, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: T cells migrate super-diffusively on scales of a few minutes.
source: The cells migrate super-diffusively on scales of a few minutes.
evidence: This is shown in the MSD analysis in Figure 1C.

claim: The MSD for a persistent random walk fits the observed data.
source: The MSD for a persistent random walk is fit to the data (Materials and methods, Appendix 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fit shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A Levy (scale-free) process consistent with the short time behavior would result in a continuation of the high frequency slope in the velocity power spectrum.
source: A Levy (scale-free) process consistent with the short time behavior would result in a continuation of the high frequency slope (dashed line).
evidence: This is based on theoretical expectations for Levy flight processes.

claim: A timescale at a few minutes is observed in the velocity power spectrum.
source: Instead, we observe a timescale at a few minutes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Each cell samples a characteristic distribution of speeds that is stable over one to two hours.
source: Thus each cell samples a characteristic distribution of speeds that is stable over one to two hours.
evidence: This is inferred from the speed correlation analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: 48% of the variance in cell speeds can be explained by the sample identity.
source: overall, 48% of the variance in cell speeds can be explained by the sample identity.
evidence: This is based on linear model fitting to the data.

claim: The distributions of cell speeds within each sample are broad and overlapping, accounting for 52% of the variance.
source: Nonetheless, the distributions of cell speeds within each sample are broad and overlapping (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), accounting for the majority of the variance (52%).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and calculated from the data.

claim: Fast cells are most likely to turn shallowly.
source: fast cells are most likely to turn shallowly
evidence: This is shown in the turn angle distributions by speed class in Figure 3A.

claim: Slow cells are most likely to turn around.
source: slow cells are most likely to turn around
evidence: This is shown in the turn angle distributions by speed class in Figure 3A.

claim: All cells go straighter during faster periods.
source: all cells go straighter during faster periods
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B where turn angle depends on local speed.

claim: For a given step size, slow cells are more likely to turn sharply.
source: but for a given step size, slow cells are more likely to turn sharply.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B where different speed classes have different relationships between local speed and turning.

claim: Faster cells appear initially more superdiffusive due to variation in turning behavior.
source: Due to the variation in turning behavior, the faster cells appear initially more superdiffusive.
evidence: This is shown in the MSD by speed class in Figure 3C.

claim: 73% of the variance in the average cosine of turn angles can be explained by cell speed.
source: In particular, 73% of the variance in the average cosine can be explained by cell speed
evidence: This is calculated from the spline fit analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 7% of variance in average cosine of turn angles is due to stochasticity.
source: with some residual variance due to the stochasticity of the process (7%)
evidence: This is calculated from variance decomposition analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 20% of variance in average cosine of turn angles is due to other unknown effects.
source: and other unknown effects (20%)
evidence: This is calculated from variance decomposition analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a linear dependence between persistence time and cell speed.
source: To determine the relationship between these two variables, we measured the persistence time, averaged along each trajectory, as a function of cell speed, and found a linear dependence (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Heterogeneity in speeds creates a broad range of effective diffusion constants, spanning 2 orders of magnitude.
source: In particular, heterogeneity in speeds creates a broad range of effective diffusion constants, spanning 2 orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The coupling between speed and persistence generates five-fold more variation in the effective diffusion constants across cells than would be expected for a uniform persistence time model.
source: The coupling between speed and persistence amplifies this effect, generating five-fold more variation in the effective diffusion constants across the cells than would be expected for a uniform persistence time model (UPT).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the SPC and UPT models in Figure 4B.

claim: The distribution of cell speeds shifted downwards in the presence of Rockout.
source: We found that the distribution of cell speeds shifted downwards
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B comparing control and Rockout-treated cells.

claim: A quantitatively similar positive relationship between speed and turning behavior is observed in the presence of Rockout.
source: but we still observed a quantitatively similar positive relationship between speed and turning behavior (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A comparing control and Rockout-treated cells.

claim: The correlation between average turn angle and cell speed holds amongst control mouse T cells.
source: We found that this correlation held amongst the control cells in both studies (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is shown through analysis of published data in Figure 5C.

claim: The correlation between average turn angle and cell speed holds amongst control Dictyostelium cells.
source: We found that this correlation held amongst the control cells in both studies (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is shown through analysis of published data in Figure 5E.

claim: A knockout of the non-canonical myosin Myo1g had a substantial effect on the distribution of cell speeds in mouse T cells.
source: In each case, the perturbation had a substantial effect on the distribution of cell speeds (Figure 5, E-F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D analyzing data from Gérard et al., 2014.

claim: A knockout of the Arp2/3 inhibitor Arpin had a substantial effect on the distribution of cell speeds in Dictyostelium.
source: In each case, the perturbation had a substantial effect on the distribution of cell speeds (Figure 5, E-F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F analyzing data from Dang et al., 2013.

claim: A quantitatively similar positive relationship between speed and turning behavior was preserved in Myo1g knockout mouse T cells.
source: However, in both cases, a quantitatively similar positive relationship between the speed and turning behavior amongst the perturbed cells was preserved.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C comparing control and Myo1g KO cells.

claim: A quantitatively similar positive relationship between speed and turning behavior was preserved in Arpin knockout Dictyostelium.
source: However, in both cases, a quantitatively similar positive relationship between the speed and turning behavior amongst the perturbed cells was preserved.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E comparing control and Arpin KO cells.

claim: 330 putative T cells were identified from single-cell RNA sequencing.
source: We used standard dimensional reduction and clustering methods (Materials and methods) to identify 330 putative T cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A population of epithelial cells may mis-express lck at low levels.
source: Unexpectedly, we also identified a population of epithelial cells that may mis-express lck at low levels (Materials and methods, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: Two main T cell subtypes were identified using self-assembling manifold algorithm.
source: We repeated the SAM analysis on the remaining (n = 237) cells, and identified two main subtypes (Figure 6A–B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A-B using SAM analysis.

claim: The two T cell subtypes are consistent with a previous report.
source: and identified two main subtypes (Figure 6A–B), consistent with a previous report (Tang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2017.

claim: Both T cell subpopulations express high levels of genes canonically involved in actin nucleation and remodeling in the leukocyte cytoskeleton.
source: Both subpopulations of cells express high levels of genes canonically involved in actin nucleation and remodeling in the leukocyte cytoskeleton (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2002; Takenawa and Suetsugu, 2007) (WASP/ARP2/3 pathway; Figure 6B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Three of the four top genes correlated with arpc1b are also canonically involved in the actin nucleation pathway.
source: We found that 3 of the four top correlated genes (those that are statistically significant after Bonferonni correction) are also canonically involved in this pathway: the actin monomer genes act2b and act1b, as well as the upstream activator cdc42l.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C through correlation analysis.

claim: The fourth gene most correlated with arpc1b encodes a lincRNA whose biological function is unknown.
source: Unexpectedly, the fourth gene encodes a lincRNA whose biological function is unknown.
evidence: This is identified in the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Co-variation is detected in genes involved with actin nucleation among T cells.
source: Thus we detect real, although not strong, co-variation in genes involved with actin nucleation, which may create long-lived cell-intrinsic variation in motility.
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The distributions of expression for arpc1b and its correlates overlap for the two T cell subtypes.
source: Indeed, the distributions of expression for the two subtypes overlap for these genes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The overlapping expression distributions are consistent with a single continuous motility axis without two distinct subgroups.
source: This is consistent with a single continuous motility axis, without two distinct subgroups, as in our microscopy data.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cells may vary along a 'nucleation high' to 'nucleation low' axis, generating a range of long-lived speed states.
source: This observation suggests that cells may vary along a 'nucleation high' to 'nucleation low' axis, generating a range of long-lived speed states.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed transcriptional heterogeneity.

claim: The statistics of zebrafish T cell trajectories closely resemble those measured by Harris et al. up through the 10 min time lag.
source: However, we note that the statistics of our trajectories closely resemble those measured by Harris et al. up through the 10 min time lag analyzed in that study.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data from Harris et al., 2012.

claim: Actin retrograde flow speed is correlated both with cell speed and persistence time.
source: Maiuri et al. also observed a coupling between speed and directional persistence across multiple cell types, and performed elegant in vitro work to demonstrate that actin retrograde flow speed is correlated both with cell speed and persistence time (Maiuri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Maiuri et al., 2015.

claim: Increasing cell speed may in many cases increase straightness, and vice versa.
source: Our analysis suggests that increasing cell speed may in many cases increase straightness, and vice versa, so that the effect on cell steering may be indirect.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed speed-persistence coupling.

claim: Spontaneous cytosolic calcium signaling generates pauses during basal T cell motility.
source: Another mechanistic basis for intermittency was demonstrated by Dong et al., 2017, who showed that spontaneous cytosolic calcium signaling generates pauses during basal T cell motility.
evidence: This is cited from Dong et al., 2017.

claim: Calcium signaling can cause cell arrest, which is important to contact with antigen presenting cells and antigen recognition.
source: We additionally note that several studies (Dustin et al., 1997; Mempel et al., 2004; Kawakami et al., 2005; Castellino et al., 2006; Moreau et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2017; Negulescu et al., 1996) have indicated that T cells react to local chemical signals by changing speed–in particular, that calcium signaling can cause cell arrest, and this is important to contact with antigen presenting cells and antigen recognition.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Imaging was performed on Tg(lck:GFP) zebrafish crossed into a nacre-/- background, at between 9 and 13 dpf.
source: Imaging was performed on Tg(lck:GFP) zebrafish crossed into a nacre-/- background, at between 9 and 13 dpf.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Tiled z-stacks were obtained every 45 s for at least 180 timepoints.
source: With the exception of Figure 2 and Figure 2—video 1, tiled z-stacks were obtained every 45 s for at least 180 timepoints
evidence: This describes the imaging protocol.

claim: Trajectories with at least 30 consecutive steps were included in the analysis.
source: Trajectories with at least 30 consecutive steps were included in the analysis
evidence: This describes the data inclusion criteria.

claim: Cells were filtered if they expressed fewer than 650 genes or more than 3250 genes in scRNA-seq analysis.
source: Cells were filtered if they expressed fewer than 650 genes or more than 3250 genes
evidence: This describes the quality control criteria for scRNA-seq data.

claim: Cells were filtered if more than 8% of reads were of mitochondrial origin in scRNA-seq analysis.
source: and if more than 8% of reads were of mitochondrial origin.
evidence: This describes the quality control criteria for scRNA-seq data.
